results.summary_before: This project implements a ring-oscillator-based physically unclonable function (PUF) with 8 bits of challenge-response pairs. It uses 32 ring oscillators per bit, selected by the challenge, and races counters to produce a response bit. The design requires no external hardware and is tested by applying challenges and observing responses, though responses may vary with temperature. The author seeks collaboration to characterize the PUF's uniqueness, reliability, and entropy across many devices.

results.summary_before: This project implements four NIST statistical tests (Frequency, Block Frequency, Runs, and Longest Run of Ones) to evaluate random bit sequences. It also includes an analog LFSR with configurable delay lines that can act as a conventional LFSR, oscillator, or chaotic oscillator. The design accepts random bits as input and outputs test results, and requires external hardware for configuration and monitoring. It is based on published works on low-cost on-chip randomness tests.

results.summary_before: This project exposes a VCO and a phase-frequency detector as building blocks of a phase-locked loop, with analog control and output pins plus digital select and clock inputs. An oscilloscope, function generator and bench power supply are suggested but not required for testing. A silicon test report confirms the VCO works, producing 13 kHz to 66 MHz, though the usable control range was 0.4 V to 1.0 V rather than the documented 1.0 V to 1.8 V. The phase-frequency detector was not tested by the reporter, and the design is notable for including measured silicon results.

results.summary_before: This is a simple Pong game where the ball is represented by an image of the Polish pope, output over VGA. It supports two players via button inputs or an AI opponent, selectable by a pin. The design requires external hardware for VGA digital-to-analog conversion, a VGA monitor, and buttons for player input. The game logic runs once per frame during vertical sync, and it outputs one pixel per clock cycle.

results.summary_before: Supermic implements an 8-channel delay-and-sum beamformer for digital microphone arrays. It accepts eight PDM microphone inputs in DDR format, converts them to single-data-rate PCM using third-order CIC filters, applies per-channel configurable delays via shift registers, and sums the results. The beamformed signal is output as an I2S stream, and individual channel PCM outputs are also provided. External hardware includes eight digital microphones, a clock generator (such as a Raspberry Pi or microcontroller), and an I2S receiver; the design is documented but has no reported silicon test results.
